title: The rise of vertical AI-native services in India
gist: An update to a 2025 roadmap on AI disrupting the $264 billion IT services industry: the NIFTY IT index is down 39% from its December 2024 peak, India's top five IT firms grew constant-currency revenue just 1.2% in FY26, and frontier labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Sarvam) are now building their own deployment businesses because incumbent SIs lack the AI talent density to close the implementation gap. The argument is that vertically specialized AI-native companies built in India and selling globally will capture the next era of enterprise services — and that gross margins track workflow complexity, not whether humans sit in the delivery loop (Palantir at 80%+ is the proof).

themes.theme: NIFTY IT drawdown and incumbent stall

insights.claim: The NIFTY IT index, which tracks India's ten largest listed IT services companies on the National Stock Exchange, had fallen 39% from its December 2024 peak as of May 2026 — one of the sharpest corrections in the sector's history.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: A 39% sectoral drawdown is the market already repricing the labor-arbitrage delivery model; the question for allocators is whether it is discounting or a value trap.
insights.quote: had fallen 39% from its December 2024 peak, one of the sharpest corrections in the sector's history
insights.locator: In May 2026, the NIFTY IT index

insights.claim: India's top five IT services companies posted average constant-currency revenue growth of just 1.2% in FY26 (year ended March 2026), one of the slowest years on record, while revenue per employee stayed flat — a trend that has now persisted for a decade.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Flat revenue per employee for ten years is the cleanest evidence that no AI productivity uplift has reached the P&L; watch this metric, not AI-first press releases.
insights.quote: the top five IT services companies posted an average constant-currency revenue growth of just 1.2%
insights.locator: Incumbents have seen tepid revenue growth

insights.claim: Incumbent IT services firms have answered the AI threat with M&A rather than model change: Capgemini acquired WNS, HCL invested in Sarvam, TCS acquired Coastal Cloud and ListEngage, and Coforge acquired Encora.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: A consolidation wave signals defensive capability-buying; screen these deals for whether acquired revenue is outcome-priced or still headcount-linked.
insights.locator: The recent selloff has been accompanied by a wave of consolidation

insights.claim: Few incumbents have disclosed the operating or financial metrics that would prove AI has structurally changed how they deliver, price, or margin their work, so their AI-first repositioning remains ambition rather than evidence of reinvention.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Treat disclosure of AI-linked delivery, pricing and margin metrics as the falsifiable trigger to re-rate an incumbent; absent it, discount the narrative.
insights.quote: the AI-first narrative remains a story about ambition rather than proof of reinvention
insights.locator: While incumbents have been quick to rebrand as AI-first

insights.claim: Incumbent IT services revenue has no installed base or subscription layer that renews by default: deals are announced as multi-year total contract value that must be re-won, re-scoped and re-staffed each cycle, so every dollar of next year's revenue must be re-sold.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: This is the structural reason the sector cannot trade on SaaS multiples — no compounding installed base means no operating leverage from AI.
insights.quote: Every dollar of next year's revenue must be re-sold.
insights.locator: Beneath those headline numbers lies a more fundamental problem

insights.claim: The most valuable AI deployments compound over time, improve with use and do not need to be re-staffed to grow — the exact inverse of a commercial model that assumes value is delivered by people, billed by the hour and renewed by the relationship.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: The mismatch between AI's compounding economics and hourly billing is the core short thesis on labor-linked services; exposure scales with headcount dependence.
insights.quote: that value is delivered by people, billed by the hour, and renewed by the relationship
insights.locator: This model is precisely the inverse of what AI makes possible

insights.claim: Bessemer's October 2025 roadmap predicted AI-native challengers would disrupt a $264 billion IT services industry, and nine months later the author says the market moved faster than even they anticipated.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: The TAM being contested is $264B; velocity of repricing has exceeded a specialist VC's own base case, which argues against waiting for confirmation.
insights.quote: AI-native challengers would disrupt this $264 billion industry
insights.locator: In October 2025, we published our roadmap

themes.theme: Frontier labs building their own deployment businesses

insights.claim: OpenAI, Anthropic and Sarvam have independently concluded that the binding constraint on AI's enterprise impact is not model intelligence but embedding that intelligence into enterprise workflows.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: If deployment, not capability, is the bottleneck, value accrues to whoever owns workflow embedding — a different asset than compute or model IP.
insights.quote: the biggest constraint on AI's impact isn't model intelligence, it's embedding that intelligence into enterprise workflows
insights.locator: Why frontier labs are now building services companies

insights.claim: Anthropic launched an AI-native enterprise services firm backed by Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman and Goldman Sachs, built around embedding applied AI engineers directly inside client organizations to rebuild workflows using Claude.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: A model lab entering forward-deployed services with PE and bank capital behind it means labs are competing for the services margin pool, not just the API line.
insights.locator: Anthropic launched an AI-native enterprise services firm

insights.claim: OpenAI created the OpenAI Deployment Company with more than $4 billion from 19 investors led by TPG, and moved to acquire applied AI consultancy Tomoro to seed it with roughly 150 deployment engineers and specialists.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: A $4bn+ separately capitalized deployment vehicle sets a price on deployment talent; it also makes AI-native services firms acquisition targets.
insights.quote: a new vehicle backed by more than $4 billion from 19 investors led by TPG
insights.locator: OpenAI followed with the OpenAI Deployment Company

insights.claim: Frontier labs are co-opting the consultancies as distribution: OpenAI's Frontier Alliance pairs its forward-deployed engineers with McKinsey, BCG, Accenture and Capgemini, while Anthropic partners with Deloitte, Accenture and Infosys with emphasis on regulated and complex industries.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Incumbent SIs are being repositioned from principal to channel — revenue may hold while the value capture and pricing power shift upstream to the labs.
insights.locator: Simultaneously, partner ecosystems are extending the reach of frontier labs

insights.claim: Sarvam AI partnered with YCP India to pair its full-stack sovereign AI platform with cross-sector expertise, deploying inside enterprises' own regulatory requirements and legacy systems within the region.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Sovereign-AI-plus-local-deployment is emerging as a distinct India go-to-market wedge that global labs cannot easily replicate on regulated workloads.
insights.locator: Sarvam AI partnered with YCP India

insights.claim: The labs built their own deployment entities not because incumbent global systems integrators lacked enterprise relationships or delivery scale, but because they lack the AI capability and talent density to close the implementation gap at the required speed.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: This reframes the moat question: enterprise relationships are no longer a defensible asset if the capability to use them is missing — bearish for SI franchise value.
insights.quote: the fastest path to deployment runs around it, not through it
insights.locator: These AI leaders did not build new deployment entities

themes.theme: Enterprise triage: build in-house, build with an SI, or buy AI-native

insights.claim: Enterprises moving from pilots to production face three distinct choices — build in-house, build with a global SI, or buy from an AI-native specialist — and the path taken depends on engineering depth, technology strategy and use-case complexity.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: This triage is the demand-side map: it tells you which layer (infra, SI, vertical specialist) captures each dollar of enterprise AI spend.
insights.locator: As enterprises move from pilots to production

insights.claim: Stripe built its own payments foundation model trained on tens of billions of transactions, lifting card-testing fraud detection at large merchants from 59% to 97% — a result that previously would have required a third-party vendor like FICO's Falcon.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: A 59%-to-97% in-house jump is a direct displacement of an incumbent risk-scoring vendor; read it as a template for data-rich firms insourcing vendor categories.
insights.quote: lifting its card-testing fraud detection rate at large merchants from 59% to 97%
insights.locator: Approach #1:- Build in-house

insights.claim: Klarna's in-house AI assistant now handles a large share of customer service interactions, doing the work of roughly 700 employees.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Quantified headcount displacement in a support function is the benchmark BPO buyers will anchor on when repricing outsourced contracts.
insights.quote: doing the work of roughly 700 employees
insights.locator: Klarna deployed an in-house AI assistant

insights.claim: As AI coding tools let small internal teams do what once required a large offshore delivery team, demand shifts away from both SIs and AI-native services firms toward the infrastructure layer beneath: coding assistants, agentic developer tools, model-serving platforms, orchestration frameworks and data infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: The second-order trade: insourcing is a headwind for services at both ends of the barbell but a direct tailwind for dev-tooling and serving/orchestration infra.
insights.quote: This shifts demand away from SIs and AI-native services firms and toward the infrastructure layer underneath
insights.locator: As AI coding tools lower the barrier to deployment

insights.claim: Global SIs are still winning large mandates: Accenture nearly doubled its generative AI bookings to $5.9 billion in FY25, and in its Telstra engagement it took on much of the Australian telco's data and AI roadmap, consolidating 18 vendors down to two and rebuilding core processes with agentic AI.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: The disruption is not instantaneous — $5.9bn of genAI bookings and vendor-consolidation mandates show incumbent SIs still have a live, sticky bid.
insights.quote: Accenture nearly doubled its generative AI bookings to $5.9 billion in FY25
insights.locator: Approach #2 : Build with a global SI

insights.claim: The SI opportunity pool is shrinking for three compounding reasons: simple use cases move in-house via tools like Claude Code, AI-native vendors productize vertical solutions that deploy faster and cost less than custom SI builds, and engineers capable of building cutting-edge AI now choose AI-native companies over incumbent SIs.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Three simultaneous squeezes — demand, price and talent — means SI erosion compounds rather than mean-reverts; the talent leg is the hardest to fix with capital.
insights.quote: the capability gap that once pushed enterprises toward the SIs is now opening up inside them
insights.locator: But this pool of opportunity is shrinking

insights.claim: Buying from an AI-native specialist beats commissioning a headcount-priced custom build where the workflow is complex, regulated and domain-heavy — named niches include pharmacovigilance, medical coding and claims, AML and KYC, and regulatory writing.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: These four verticals are the author's explicit hunting list for where AI-native challengers can take share fastest — a concrete sourcing screen.
insights.quote: vertical niches such as pharmacovigilance, medical coding and claims, AML and KYC, regulatory writing
insights.locator: Approach #3: Buy from an AI-native specialist

insights.claim: The line between software and services is blurring: enterprises are no longer choosing between a tool and a vendor but deciding how to deliver outcomes, making 'buy' the rational default for a widening set of complex vertical workflows.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Outcome-buying erodes the software-versus-services taxonomy that underpins current sector multiples — expect classification and comp-set disputes.
insights.quote: Enterprises are not choosing between a tool and a vendor, but ultimately how to deliver outcomes
insights.locator: But the lines between software and services are blurring

themes.theme: The four-model grid for vertical AI vendors

insights.claim: Vertical AI-native business models can be mapped on two axes: whether the customer buys a tool to operate or a finished outcome, and whether it is delivered as software alone or software plus people — yielding copilots, autopilots, platform-plus-delivery, and AI-native services.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: A clean diligence grid: place any AI company on it to predict its gross-margin profile, accountability exposure and likely migration path.
insights.quote: Does the customer buy a tool to operate or a finished outcome?
insights.locator: Four business models, all capable of software margins

insights.claim: The four models have concrete exemplars: Cursor as the software-led copilot where the engineer reviews every change, Kintsugi as the autopilot that registers, files and remits sales tax with no human in the loop, Wonderful AI as platform-plus-delivery with forward-deployed engineers, and Crosby as a vertically integrated AI law firm taking professional responsibility for signed-off contracts.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Each name is a comparable for a distinct margin and liability archetype — useful when benchmarking a private AI company's model against the right peer.
insights.locator: Business models of Vertical AI-Native solutions

insights.claim: Companies migrate across the business-model grid as AI capability improves — coding assistance is a copilot while the engineer drives every decision and becomes an autopilot once an agent completes the task independently — converting delivery effort into reusable product and gaining margin leverage as they go.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Model-grid migration is the value-creation path to underwrite: buy services-led businesses that are visibly productizing delivery, not those static in the labor quadrant.
insights.quote: companies tend to move across the grid, converting delivery effort into reusable products and gaining margin leverage as they go
insights.locator: These models are not mutually exclusive

themes.theme: Margins track complexity, not the delivery model

insights.claim: The intuition that pure autopilot software with no humans in the delivery loop is the highest-margin, most defensible model is wrong: margins track the complexity of the work, not the delivery model.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Undermines the reflex discount applied to any AI company with a services line — complexity of workflow, not headcount, should drive the margin assumption.
insights.quote: margins don’t track the delivery model - they track the complexity of the work
insights.locator: The instinctive read of this framework

insights.claim: Palantir is a services-led, platform-plus-delivery business with forward-deployed engineers embedded in every significant deployment, yet earns gross margins north of 80% because the work is complex, deeply embedded and hard to replicate.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: The existence proof that FDE-heavy delivery can sustain 80%+ gross margins — the key comp for underwriting AI-native services valuations.
insights.quote: The company earns gross margins north of 80, because the work is complex, deeply embedded, and hard to replicate.
insights.locator: Palantir is the counterexample that settles the question

insights.claim: Removing people from delivery does not guarantee software-like margins: basic AI customer-service chat is commoditizing, with prices and margins falling despite requiring little human involvement.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: A short-side screen: low-complexity, fully automated AI point solutions face price deflation, not margin expansion.
insights.quote: Basic AI customer-service chat is becoming commoditized, driving prices and margins down despite requiring little human involvement.
insights.locator: The opposite is also true

themes.theme: Five levers to software-like gross margins in AI services

insights.claim: Owning the end outcome rather than automating one slice of a workflow is what converts a vendor from a feature into infrastructure, and a customer relying on a vendor for a result is far harder to displace than one using it to speed up a task they still own.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Outcome ownership is the retention variable to diligence — it predicts net revenue retention better than product features.
insights.quote: Automate one slice of a workflow and you are a feature. Own the end outcome and you are infrastructure.
insights.locator: 1. Own the workflow

insights.claim: Graph AI owns the entire pharmacovigilance and regulatory affairs workflow — case intake and processing, aggregate reporting, signal detection and risk management — delivering validated safety reports submitted to country-specific regulatory databases rather than an input toward them.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: A concrete template for end-to-end vertical ownership in a regulated workflow; the submission endpoint is where the value and the lock-in sit.
insights.locator: Graph AI applies this in pharmacovigilance

insights.claim: A learning loop where every human-resolved exception becomes a training signal makes the business cheaper to run as it grows — Wonderful's customer-service agents raise the share of cases resolved unaided over time, lowering human cost per deployment.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Ask for the unaided-resolution rate curve by cohort: a rising curve is the observable proof of a real learning loop versus a services business in disguise.
insights.quote: The business gets cheaper to run as it grows.
insights.locator: 2. Build the learning loop

insights.claim: Cost to serve should fall with volume by routing the straightforward majority of requests to smaller or fine-tuned models, reserving frontier models for the hard tail, and caching repeated work — making margin expansion a function of scale rather than a ceiling imposed by it.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Model routing and caching architecture is now a margin driver, not an engineering detail — a diligence item for any high-volume agent business.
insights.quote: Margin expansion becomes a function of scale rather than a ceiling imposed by it.
insights.locator: 3. Drive down the cost to serve

insights.claim: Reuse across deployments spreads the fixed costs of integrations, security, compliance and model operations across the customer base; Aivar distilled delivery accelerators from individual client engagements into reusable IP so each new deployment is increasingly an assembly of existing components.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Falling marginal cost per new customer is the metric that separates a compounding platform from a bespoke consultancy.
insights.quote: The marginal cost of a new customer falls with every customer added.
insights.locator: 4. Reuse across deployments

insights.claim: AI-native delivery inverts the large, junior-heavy pyramid of incumbent IT services: skill density rather than headcount carries the work, as with Tessera delivering ERP modernization programs that once required large consulting teams using a small AI-native team.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Revenue per head is the single comparable that will separate AI-native services from legacy SIs — track it as the sector's new scoreboard.
insights.quote: Skill density, not headcount, is what carries the work.
insights.locator: 5. Deliver with a small, high-skill team

themes.theme: Founder playbook: what makes a vertical AI position durable

insights.claim: With foundation models widely accessible, open-source alternatives improving and demo-building costs falling, a polished proof-of-concept on commodity models is table stakes rather than a differentiator.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Discount any AI pitch whose evidence is a demo; the defensibility question has moved entirely downstream of model access.
insights.quote: A polished proof-of-concept built on commodity models is no longer a differentiator, it truly is table stakes.
insights.locator: How to win as a verticalized player

insights.claim: Durable vertical positions are built on workflows with high complexity, dense edge cases and real consequences on failure — dCortex runs AI agents that reason, coordinate and act across airline operations in real time, where complexity is the moat rather than a cost of operating.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Invert the usual screen: prefer messy, high-consequence workflows precisely because they resist thin foundation-model wrappers.
insights.quote: Complexity is not a cost of operating in this market; it is the moat.
insights.locator: 1. Solve a problem that is hard enough to matter

insights.claim: The lasting advantage in vertical AI is proprietary domain knowledge layered on top of models, not model quality — EvenUp's personal-injury platform is trained on hundreds of thousands of injury cases and millions of medical records, a corpus a rival cannot assemble overnight.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Proprietary corpus depth, measured in cases and records, is the asset to underwrite in vertical AI — not benchmark scores.
insights.quote: any well-funded competitor can access the same frontier models
insights.locator: 2. Embed domain knowledge a competitor cannot quickly reconstruct

insights.claim: Distribution through the enterprise system of record beats rip-and-replace: Abridge is the first health IT vendor accepted into Epic's Partners and Pals program and runs natively inside the standard Epic workflow, so AI-generated visit notes appear directly in the patient chart.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: System-of-record partnership status is a distribution moat that compounds — check for it when comparing otherwise similar vertical AI vendors.
insights.quote: Distribution through the system of record is what allows Abridge to spread across an entire health system in a way a rip-and-replace product never could.
insights.locator: 3. Build on top of systems of record, not against them

insights.claim: In regulated industries compliance is the price of admission, and owning the regulatory submission path plus the audit trail behind it makes a vendor extremely hard to remove — Graph AI's platform is built around the frameworks and submission formats governing global drug safety, enabling filings with the FDA and EMA.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Switching cost expressed as regulatory risk is the strongest retention mechanism in vertical AI; prioritize vendors that own the filing endpoint.
insights.quote: switching is becomes a regulatory risk a drug-safety team will not casually take
insights.locator: 4. Own the regulatory and compliance layer

insights.claim: Speed is a structural moat in vertical AI because early deployments generate proprietary data, that data improves the model, a better model wins the next customer, and the cycle repeats — so companies that become the default in a vertical now impose escalating costs on later entrants.
insights.speaker: Priya Kale
insights.so_what: Enterprises are making long-term vendor decisions right now, so the vertical-AI land-grab window is closing — favor speed of GTM over feature completeness in underwriting.
insights.quote: In vertical AI, speed becomes a structural moat to lay claim on product innovation and market leadership.
insights.locator: 5. Get speedy to compound the lead
